title: Study Abroad Experience at Gdansk
paragraphs: I am 中村里香, and from March 2019 I was allowed to study abroad for about two and a half months at the Medical University of Gdansk in Poland. I was able to have valuable experiences that I could not have had in my life until now, and I feel my horizons have greatly broadened. At the same time, I was able to realize a dream I had had since entering university, and felt a sense of accomplishment that could not be greater. Based on this study abroad, I would like to write about the clerkships at the Medical University of Gdansk and daily life.

The Medical University of Gdansk has two courses, the Polish Division and the English Division. Although the official language is Polish, we were allowed to do clerkships in the latter, so we could study medicine in English. Also, because it targets exchange students from various countries, I was able to become friends with students from countries I had never met anyone from before. Specifically they were Sweden, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, India, Spain, Italy and so on. Because I was mixed into clinical clerkship groups where such students gathered, I could talk about all sorts of things every day, and it was a very valuable experience. In particular, seeing many students in the class who looked unwell because of Ramadan, I came to feel Islam closer than before. It was also surprising that every student knew a lot about their own country's culture and history, and some understood Japan more deeply than I do.

I rotated through pulmonology, ophthalmology, tropical medicine and infectious diseases, and medical oncology, one to two weeks each. There was a test at the end of every department, which was hard, but I attended classes with an electronic dictionary in hand and asked students about the content, so I was able to tackle the clerkship more seriously. In particular, in pulmonology the exercise of reading images and answering orally one by one was nerve-racking but became a very good memory. In tropical medicine and infectious diseases I was able to meet patients with malaria and echinococcus, which I had never seen in Japan, and see a variety of cases.

When I arrived at the beginning of March, of course, and even in mid-May when I left, it was so cold that Heattech was essential. But in the latter half I was able to see cherry blossoms in full bloom and feel the arrival of spring.
It is so safe that even we could go out at night. Prices are about a third, very cheap, and my eyes lit up every time at the supermarkets and restaurants. It was a place easy for students to live in.

Professor Wozniak, a professor of biochemistry who loves Japan very much, supported us at every turn. From the time we arrived he welcomed us, saying, "I am like a father to you in Poland, so contact me about anything if you have trouble," and I still remember that it dispelled the anxiety I had felt about my new life ahead. Invited by the professor, I was also able to have the valuable experience of wearing a kimono he lent me and giving a presentation in English on green tea in front of high school students. I was also frequently introduced to his wife Maria and his grandchildren, and was taken to an Easter party with homemade food and to a delicious sushi restaurant. Being given such warm hospitality for our short stay, I was able to deeply understand the meaning of ichigo ichie (a once-in-a-lifetime encounter), the professor's motto. Adam, who studies under the professor, also supported us not only in the little details of daily life but also mentally as a fun conversation partner. We have countless memories, such as eating together in the cafeteria and cycling and relaxing in parks.

A meeting called each1 teach1 is held every week, whose aim is for exchange students to learn each other's languages and widen their circle of friends, and I had the opportunity to teach Japanese to friends. Students from other faculties who study at other universities also come there. When I explained the use of hiragana, katakana and kanji, that infinite kanji exist even for the same sound, and that we use honorific language in ordinary life, they held their heads in their hands at the difficulty, and I realized that the language I use is more difficult than I had imagined.

It was the most fulfilling two and a half months of my life so far. For me, who was living alone and staying abroad for a long time for the first time, every day was very stimulating. And what I felt most strongly through this study abroad was the generosity of everyone who tried to accept and entertain us even though we were strangers staying only a short time. I had not done anything like that for the exchange students who had come to my university until now, so I reflected deeply. By experiencing, for the first time, being a minority and touching everyone's warm hearts, it was an important period in which I wanted to change how I had been until now and make use of it in the future.

I thank the professors of the International Collaboration Office, the professors of the Medical University of Gdansk, the alumni doctors of the Frontier Association, everyone at Academic Affairs, 鷲見, who studied abroad with me, my family, and various other people, who gave great support over a long time from the preparation period before study abroad until after my return. Thank you.
